title: Where are you from?
topic: מֵאֵיפֹה; prefixes מִ־ בְּ־; nationalities m./f.
why: After pronouns and jobs, you learn to say where you're from and where you live, with the little attached words מִ (from) and בְּ (in). Nationalities in the masculine and feminine complete your introduction.

{"lessons": ["

Where are you from?

You know אֵיפֹה (eifo, where?). Attach מֵ (from) to it and you get מֵאֵיפֹה (me-eifo): where from? As always, no verb: literally \"from where you?\"

מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה? / מֵאֵיפֹה אַתְּ?Where are you from? (to a man / to a woman) [me-eifo ata? / me-eifo at?]
אֲנִי מִצָּרְפַת, מִפָּרִיז.I'm from France, from Paris. [ani mi-tsarfat, mi-pariz]

To say where you live, learn this expression as a whole. The word גָּר is a verb: you'll see all its forms in unit 5. For now, just remember that a man says גָּר (gar) and a woman says גָּרָה (gara).

אֵיפֹה אַתָּה גָּר? / אֵיפֹה אַתְּ גָּרָה?Where do you live? (to a man / to a woman) [eifo ata gar? / eifo at gara?]
אֲנִי גָּרָה בְּתֵל אָבִיב.I live in Tel Aviv. (a woman speaking) [ani gara be-tel aviv]

To add a nuance: אֲנִי מִפָּרִיז, אֲבָל אֲנִי גָּר בְּתֵל אָבִיב. The word אֲבָל (aval) means \"but.\"

", "

Two little attached words: בְּ and מִ

English says \"in Paris,\" \"in France\" and \"from Paris,\" \"from France,\" with a separate word. Hebrew also has just one word for each idea, but it is always glued to the front of the noun, and there is never an article before a country:

PrefixMeaningExample
בְּ (be)in, at: where you areבְּתֵל אָבִיב, בְּצָרְפַת, בְּקָנָדָה
מִ (mi)from: where you come fromמִתֵּל אָבִיב, מִצָּרְפַת, מִקָּנָדָה

Look closely at מִ: it adds a dot (dagesh) to the next letter. That's why מִפָּרִיז is read mi-pariz, with a real p.

Before א, ה, ח, ע and ר, which don't take that dot, מִ becomes מֵ (me):

מֵאִיטַלְיָה, מֵחֵיפָה, מֵרוֹמָאfrom Italy, from Haifa, from Rome [me-italya, me-kheifa, me-roma]

Jerusalem gets shortened in speech: בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם is said birushalayim (in Jerusalem), and מִירוּשָׁלַיִם mirushalayim (from Jerusalem).

", "

Nationalities

Nationalities are adjectives: they agree with the person. The masculine ends in ִי (i); the feminine in ִיָּה (iya) or in ִית (it). You have to learn which one, word by word.

CountryMasculineFeminine
צָרְפַת tsarfatצָרְפָתִי tsarfatiצָרְפָתִיָּה tsarfatiya
יִשְׂרָאֵל yisra'elיִשְׂרְאֵלִי yisre'eliיִשְׂרְאֵלִית yisre'elit
אִיטַלְיָה italyaאִיטַלְקִי italkiאִיטַלְקִיָּה italkiya
גֶּרְמַנְיָה germanyaגֶּרְמָנִי germaniגֶּרְמָנִיָּה germaniya
קָנָדָה kanadaקָנָדִי kanadiקָנָדִית kanadit
אָמֶרִיקָה amerikaאֲמֵרִיקָאִי amerika'iאֲמֵרִיקָאִית amerika'it
רוֹן יִשְׂרְאֵלִי, וְנֹעָה צָרְפָתִיָּה.Ron is Israeli, and Noa is French. [Ron yisre'eli, ve-No'a tsarfatiya]

Hebrew has no capital letters: not for countries, not for names, not for nationalities (which English capitalizes). And in conversation you'll often hear israeli rather than yisre'eli.
